orders.description: Defendants’ appeal from the June 18, 2009 summary-judgment denial.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendants’ motion to dismiss the complaint on summary judgment.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on ice in the parking lot of an apartment building owned by Norstar and managed by Siara. The parties disputed whether the fall involved preexisting ice or recently fallen snow.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants established an ongoing storm, but plaintiff’s expert affidavit and weather reports raised a triable issue whether the ice predated it. Her deposition also raised an issue whether she fell on preexisting ice rather than recent snow.
The court rejected defendants’ claimed showing that recent snow, rather than previously formed ice, caused the fall; plaintiff’s deposition raised a factual issue.
The detailed meteorologist affidavit, with accompanying weather reports, raised a factual issue about ice formation before the storm; formation timing was not conclusively decided.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff submitted a detailed meteorologist affidavit supporting the preexisting-ice issue.
Weather reports accompanied the meteorologist affidavit; specific readings are not reproduced.
Plaintiff’s deposition raised an issue about ice versus recently fallen snow.

quality.notes: Apartment ownership/management supports the private parking lot. Plaintiff’s tenancy and accident date are unstated. Triable preexisting ice does not establish notice or liability. Affirmance of denial favors plaintiff.

evidence.quote: It is hereby ordered that the order so appealed from is unanimously affirmed without costs.

Plaintiff commenced this action seeking damages for injuries she sustained when she allegedly slipped and fell on ice in the parking lot of an apartment building owned by defendant Norstar Apartments, LLC and managed by defendant Siara Management, Inc.

Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Onondaga County (John C. Cherundolo, A.J.), entered June 18, 2009 in a personal injury action. The order denied defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing plaintiffs complaint.
Although defendants met their initial burden of establishing as a matter of law that there was a storm in progress at the time of the accident

the evidence submitted by plaintiff, particularly the detailed affidavit from her expert meteorologist and the accompanying weather reports, raised an issue of fact whether the ice in question had formed prior to commencement of the storm

We reject defendants’ further contention that they are entitled to summary judgment because they established that plaintiff fell on snow that had recently fallen rather than ice previously formed. Plaintiff’s deposition testimony was sufficient to raise an issue of fact in that regard as well.
We conclude that Supreme Court properly denied defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Defendants’ appeal from the June 23, 2016 summary-judgment denial.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff alleged a trip into a grass-covered hole on defendants’ property. She attributed the hole or small ditch to gutter runoff from the back of the home toward a creek; that formation theory was her contention.

legal_issues.finding: Imposing an inspection duty was error because nothing aroused defendants’ suspicions; that error did not eliminate the triable issues barring summary judgment.
Defendants failed to establish noncreation as a matter of law; plaintiff’s gutter-runoff theory was not conclusively established.
Defendants asserted lack of actual notice below but abandoned that ground on appeal; the appellate court did not decide its substantive merits.

Defendants failed to establish lack of constructive notice. Their evidence showed visibility to at least one person and sufficient duration for discovery and remedy; the decision leaves triable issues, not final liability.

Actual notice was abandoned on appeal. Even assuming the runoff theory was not discernible from the pleadings, defendants’ initial burden failure required denial; the inspection-duty error did not change the result.

quality.notes: Owned property and the home/runoff account support private residential premises. Ground location is other: no path or sidewalk is stated. No evidence format, injured role or accident date is supplied. Pleading and inspection issues are ancillary to negligence merits; no definitive creation/notice finding is inferred.

evidence.quote: It is hereby ordered that the order so appealed from is unanimously affirmed without costs.
Plaintiff commenced this action seeking damages for injuries she sustained when she tripped and fell on property owned by defendants.
Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Erie County (E. Jeannette Ogden, J.), entered June 23, 2016. The order denied defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing plaintiff’s complaint.

Here, the evidence submitted by defendants established that the condition was visible and apparent to at least one person and that the condition had existed for a sufficient length of time for defendants to have discovered and remedied it.

In her complaint, plaintiff alleged that she fell after she stepped in a hole in the ground that was covered by grass, and that defendants knew or should have known that the dangerous condition existed on their property.

In opposition to defendants’ motion and on appeal, plaintiff contends, inter aha, that defendants created the hole “by allowing water to run off from the gutter in the back of [the] home toward the creek and thus creating a small ditch that ultimately became a tripping hazard.”

Even assuming, arguendo, that plaintiff’s opposition to the motion set forth a theory of recovery that was “not readily discernible from the allegations in the complaint and the original bill of particulars” (Rosse-Glickman v Beth Israel Med. Ctr.-Kings Hwy. Div., 309 AD2d 846, 846 [2003]), we nevertheless conclude that defendants’ motion was properly denied inasmuch as defendants failed to establish as a matter of law that they did not *1513 create the allegedly dangerous condition or that they lacked constructive notice of it.

Moreover, while we agree with defendants that the court erred in imposing a duty to inspect the property where, as here, there was nothing to arouse defendants’ suspicions (see Anderson v Justice, 96 AD3d 1446, 1447-1448 [2012]), that error does not affect our determination that there are triable issues of fact precluding summary judgment.
We note at the outset that defendants have “abandoned any issue with respect to actual notice by failing to raise any such issue on appeal”
Defendants moved for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, contending that they neither created the dangerous condition nor had actual or constructive notice of it.
We conclude that Supreme Court properly denied defendant’s motion, but our reasoning differs from that of the court.

orders.description: Plaintiffs’ limited appeal from denial of their liability summary-judgment motion against Stop & Shop.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied the branch seeking summary judgment on liability against Stop & Shop.

facts.factual_summary: The injured plaintiff allegedly slipped in a puddle of unspecified liquid while shopping inside a Stop & Shop supermarket. Plaintiffs attributed the puddle to nearby frozen-food boxes, but this was their disputed theory.

legal_issues.finding: Plaintiffs failed to establish defendant’s creation of the puddle: their proposed leak from nearby frozen-food boxes was wholly speculative. The burden therefore never shifted to defendant.
The claimed causal link between nearby frozen-food boxes and the puddle was speculative; the opinion does not find that plaintiff could not identify the puddle as the immediate cause of her slip.

quality.notes: The supermarket interior supports private business control without asserting title or lease. Shopping supports customer status. Unspecified liquid is other, not assumed water; no evidence format is identified. General duty/notice standards do not establish separate case findings. Affirmance denies plaintiffs’ motion, not their underlying claim. Source caption says Dina but narrative says Diana; retain source metadata and do not resolve externally. This 2023 opinion receives unchanged rules.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs.

The plaintiff Diana Cashwell (hereinafter the injured plaintiff) allegedly was injured when she slipped and fell in a puddle of liquid while shopping at a Stop & Shop supermarket located in East Northport. The plaintiffs subsequently commenced this action against, among others, Stop & Shop Supermarket Company, LLC (hereinafter the defendant), seeking to recover damages for personal injuries and loss of services.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, etc., the plaintiffs appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (Joseph A. Santorelli, J.), dated November 9, 2020. The order, insofar as appealed from, denied that branch of the plaintiffs' motion which was for summary judgment on the issue of liability against the defendant Stop & Shop Supermarket Company, LLC.

Here, the plaintiffs failed to establish, prima facie, that the defendant created the condition that caused her to fall. The plaintiffs' contention that nearby boxes of frozen food had leaked and caused the puddle in which she fell was wholly speculative and, thus, insufficient to establish a prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law
Since the plaintiffs failed to meet their initial burden as the movant, the burden never shifted to the defendant to raise a triable issue of fact
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied that branch of the plaintiffs' motion which was for summary judgment on the issue of liability against the defendant.

orders.description: Plaintiff’s limited appeal concerning dismissal against the Jean Jacques defendants in the January 8, 2015 order.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted summary judgment dismissing the complaint against the caterer and its catering director.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly tripped over a black metal box between tables at a wedding reception on May 7, 2011, at premises allegedly owned by the church. The bride and groom hired the Jean Jacques caterer and its catering director for the reception.

legal_issues.finding: The catering defendants established no ownership, occupancy, control or special use of the premises and no creation through their catering work; plaintiff raised no triable issue.
The catering defendants demonstrated noncreation through their catering efforts; plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue.

The court examined the hired caterers’ premises relationship and whether their contractual catering efforts created the condition. They established neither a premises relationship imposing duty nor creation; no separate Espinal exception analysis is supplied.

quality.notes: Express alleged church ownership supports private religious premises under the codebook. Lack of caterer control does not make the site public. Owner describes the church; contractor/other describe caterer/director. Only the caterers’ dismissal is appealed, so full affirmance of that branch is 0. This is plaintiff’s direct negligence claim, not third-party-only indemnification. No evidence formats are specified.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs.

On May 7, 2011, while attending a wedding reception at a facility in Rye (hereinafter the subject premises), the plaintiff allegedly was injured when she tripped and fell over a black metal box located on the floor between two tables. The subject premises allegedly were owned by the defendant Greek Orthodox Church of Our Savior.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals, as limited by her brief, from so much of an order of the Supreme Court, Westchester County (Wood, J.), dated January 8, 2015, as granted that branch of the motion of the defendants Jean Jacques' Culinary Creations, Inc., and Mary Scelsi which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against them.

At the time of the accident, the defendants Jean Jacques' Culinary Creations, Inc., and Mary Scelsi, its catering director (hereinafter together the Jean Jacques defendants), had been hired by the nonparty bride and groom to cater the wedding at the subject premises.

Here, in support of their motion, the Jean Jacques defendants established, prima facie, that they did not own, occupy, control, or put to a special use the subject premises at the time of the accident.

Moreover, in support of their motion the Jean Jacques defendants demonstrated that they did not create the alleged dangerous condition through any efforts they undertook with respect to [*2] their obligations to cater the subject wedding. In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted that branch of the Jean Jacques defendants' motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against them.

orders.description: Plaintiff’s appeal from the May 4, 2020 summary-judgment dismissal.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on an interior staircase at premises owned by defendant and leased to the third-party defendant. The particular hazard, premises use and plaintiff’s role are unstated.

legal_issues.finding: The owner established she was out of possession and not obliged by contract or course of conduct to maintain the premises; no statutory violation was alleged and plaintiff raised no triable issue.

Defendant established the out-of-possession defense to this common-law negligence claim, with no contractual/course-of-conduct maintenance duty or alleged statutory violation; opposition raised no factual issue.

quality.notes: Express ownership and leasing support private premises. Owner is the main defendant; tenant is the third-party defendant. Stairs are location, not proof of a stair/handrail defect. No lease document or testimony format is identified. The third-party caption does not alter the direct negligence merits. No statutory violation is alleged; do not invent a code issue. This 2022 opinion receives unchanged rules.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.

The plaintiff commenced this action to recover damages for personal injuries she allegedly sustained when she slipped and fell on a staircase inside premises owned by the defendant and leased to the third-party defendant.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (William B. Rebolini, J.), dated May 4, 2020. The order granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

Here, where the complaint sounds in common-law negligence and the plaintiff does not allege the violation of a statute, the defendant demonstrated her prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law dismissing the complaint by establishing that she was an out-of-possession landlord who was not bound by contract or course of conduct to maintain the premises
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact.
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
